source: Mertens et al. (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions
finding: Large pooled meta-analysis finds a medium nudge effect before bias correction.
numbers: 455 effect sizes, 214 publications, N=2,149,683. Cohen d=0.45 (0.42 in the bias section after model refit). I2=99.67%, tau2=0.23. 95% prediction interval [-0.48, 1.39]: about 15% of nudges are expected to backfire.
limits: Egger b=2.28 shows publication bias; many studies are online or lab, some hypothetical.
agent_relevance: Expect any layout nudge to have a wide spread of effects, including reversals. Test per task; do not assume the sign.

source: Mertens et al. (2022) The effectiveness of nudging: meta-analysis of choice architecture interventions (moderators)
finding: Structure nudges (defaults, effort, option range) beat information and assistance nudges. Defaults were the strongest single technique.
numbers: Category d: structure 0.55 (k=227), information 0.38 (k=130), assistance 0.31 (k=98). Technique d: default 0.62 (k=132, N=139,948), reminder 0.30, translation 0.31, commitment 0.30, composition 0.55. Domain d: food 0.72, health 0.34, finance 0.25.
limits: Moderator tests were not corrected for publication bias. Location (US vs non-US) and population (adults vs children) did not matter (p=.60, .26).
agent_relevance: Changing what is pre-selected or how the option set is built moves choice more than adding information. For an agent, the default slot or first item is the strongest layout lever.

source: Maier, Bartos, Stanley, Shanks, Harris, Wagenmakers (2022) No evidence for nudging after adjusting for publication bias
finding: Re-analysis of the Mertens data with robust Bayesian meta-analysis (RoBMA) shrinks the mean effect to near zero.
numbers: Combined d: 0.43 raw, 0.04 [0.00,0.14] RoBMA, 0.11 [0.00,0.24] using most precise estimates; BF01=0.95 and 0.31 (undecided). Information 0.25 to 0.00 (BF01 33.8); assistance 0.22 to 0.01 (BF01 9.1); structure 0.58 to 0.12 [0.00,0.43] (BF01 1.1, undecided). Finance 0.23 to 0.00 (BF01 41). Food 0.66 to 0.02. Strong evidence of publication bias (BFpb>10).
quote: Strikingly, there is an absence of evidence for an overall effect and evidence against an effect in the 'information' and 'assistance' intervention categories
limits: Letter, not a full paper. Absence of evidence is not evidence of zero: structure nudges stay undecided. Heterogeneity is real in all categories, so some nudges work.
agent_relevance: The famous effect sizes are inflated. Plan for small average effects; the sign and size of a layout effect must be measured on our own tasks.

source: Mertens, Herberz, Hahnel, Brosch (2022) Reply to Maier et al., Szaszi et al., Bakdash and Marusich
finding: Original authors accept that publication bias exists. Their own sensitivity analysis gave smaller effects. Other methods in the three letters give smaller or null effects.
numbers: Egger b=2.10 [1.31,2.89]. Sensitivity: d=0.31 under moderate bias, d=0.08 under severe bias (the original paper text says 0.03). Raw d=0.43.
limits: They note the corpus lacked data to test many moderators. They call for preregistered reports and published nulls.
agent_relevance: Treat the true average nudge as somewhere between 0 and 0.3 d. The debate is about size, not about heterogeneity.

source: DellaVigna & Linos (2022) RCTs to Scale: Comprehensive Evidence from Two Nudge Units (NBER w27594)
finding: At-scale government nudge trials show effects about six times smaller than published academic nudge papers.
numbers: 126 RCTs, over 23 million people. Nudge Units: 1.4 pp (s.e. 0.3), 8.1% over control 17.2 pp. Academic journals (26 papers, 74 nudges): 8.7 pp (s.e. 2.5), 33.5% over control 26.0 pp. Median treatment arm: 10,006 vs 484 people; minimum detectable effect 0.8 vs 6.3 pp.
limits: Nudge Units largely avoid default changes, which are stronger. Nudges are mostly letters and emails, take-up outcomes only. Forecasters (median 4 pp) overpredicted; practitioners 1.95 pp.
agent_relevance: Published prompt-layout tricks from small benchmarks likely overstate effects. Use large test sets before adopting a prompt layout rule.

source: DellaVigna & Linos (2022) publication bias channel
finding: Selective publication plus low power explains the whole gap between academic and at-scale effects.
numbers: Non-significant trials published with estimated probability 0.1 (s.e. 0.1). Bias-corrected academic mean 3.2 pp (s.e. 1.9) vs raw 8.6 pp. More than 4 times as many published studies have t between 1.96 and 2.96 as just below.
limits: Model-based estimate; also finds some selective publication within Nudge Unit papers. Academic involvement did not explain the gap.
agent_relevance: Report all layout variants tried, not only winners, in our own experiments.

source: Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber, Johnson (2019) When and why defaults influence decisions: a meta-analysis of default effects (figure as cited in Hoang et al. 2024)
finding: Defaults reliably raise choice of the default option, with large heterogeneity. Cited effect is d=0.68.
numbers: d=0.68, 95% CI [0.53, 0.83] as quoted by the 2024 default paper. Not read directly (the Cambridge download returned only a one-page stub).
limits: Second-hand figure; pre-dates the Maier correction. Moderators (endorsement, effort, loss aversion) not verified this session.
agent_relevance: Defaults work partly because they signal endorsement. A prompt that marks one option as recommended acts the same way for a model.

source: Framing the Default (2024), preregistered test of framing x default, 1,072 US participants
finding: Choose-versus-reject framing had a strong effect in work and health scenarios. Default setting had a small effect in work and none in health.
numbers: N=1,072 analysed (1,110 completed; CloudResearch; six conditions, 175 per condition planned). Work scenario: framing OR=0.46 [0.29,0.72] p<.001; default condition 2 OR=0.49 [0.31,0.76] p=.002. Choose frame picked the 'more vacation days' job 69.1% on average. Health: no default effect.
limits: Hypothetical scenarios, online sample. Authors say the null health result mirrors other recent work.
agent_relevance: Framing (wording the same choice as choose vs reject) can matter more than a default. Always test both wordings of a decision prompt.

source: Same paper: three accounts of the default effect
finding: Rival explanations: effort, endorsement (default read as a recommendation), and status quo or loss aversion.
numbers: Cites McKenzie et al. 2006, Brown & Krishna 2004, Samuelson & Zeckhauser 1988. No single account is shown to win in this paper.
limits: Review text, not a discriminating experiment here.
agent_relevance: For an LLM the endorsement account is the closest: text that marks an option is read as advice. Effort has no direct analogue.

source: Zheng et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models Are Not Robust Multiple Choice Selectors
finding: Models prefer certain answer letters. Moving the correct answer to a different slot changes accuracy a lot.
numbers: 20 LLMs, 3 benchmarks. 0-shot MMLU gpt-3.5-turbo 67.2 original, 60.9 when gold moved to D (-6.3). llama-30B 53.1 original, +15.2 when gold moved to A (68.2 vs gpt-3.5 65.3). With 250 gold answers each of A/B/C/D, llama-30B picks A/B/C/D 34.6/27.3/22.3/15.8%.
limits: Mostly open models of 2023; multiple choice with letter IDs.
agent_relevance: Option order in a prompt is a nudge that can swing accuracy by 6 to 15 points. Randomize or permute order and aggregate.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) mechanism and fix (PriDe)
finding: The bias comes mainly from the letter tokens (token bias), not only the position. A cheap fix estimates the prior from a few permuted samples.
numbers: Relabelling to a/b/c/d, 1/2/3/4, (A)(B)(C)(D) did not remove it (gpt-3.5 MMLU recall std 5.5, 6.8, 3.8 for the three relabels or default as listed). PriDe uses about 5% of samples to estimate the prior; estimate stable from 2% to 20%. PriDe beats full or cyclic permutation at low cost.
limits: Remaining position bias after removing IDs depends on model and task.
agent_relevance: Cheap debiasing: permute a small share of items, estimate the bias, subtract it. Fits a program-run step.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators
finding: Swapping the order of two answers flips the judge's verdict. Telling the judge to ignore order did not fix it.
numbers: Vicuna-13B beats ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries when ChatGPT judges with order favouring Vicuna. Vicuna win rate 2.5% in one slot vs 82.5% in the other (ChatGPT judge). Conflict rate GPT-4 46.3% and 5.0% (two comparisons); ChatGPT 82.5% and 52.5%.
limits: Small benchmark (80 questions), 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Never let one ordered pairwise judgment decide. Swap order and average.

source: Wang et al. (2023) calibration results
finding: Evidence-first scoring plus order balancing raises agreement with humans and cuts conflicts.
numbers: ChatGPT scoring: vanilla acc 44.4%, kappa 0.06, conflict 82.5%; with multiple-evidence calibration (MEC) 53.2%, kappa 0.24, conflict 35.0%; MEC plus balanced position calibration 58.7%, kappa 0.31. Best k=3 evidence samples.
limits: Human labels from three authors; one model family.
agent_relevance: Order swap plus several evidence samples is a tested remedy that fits our operators.

source: Shi et al. (2025) Judging the Judges: position bias in LLM-as-a-Judge
finding: Position bias in judges is not random noise. It depends on the judge, the task and the quality gap between candidates.
numbers: 15 judges, MT-Bench and DevBench, 22 tasks, about 40 solution models, over 150,000 evaluations. Repetition stability above 0.95 for Claude-3.5-Sonnet, GPT-4, Llama-3.3-70B. Bias is tied to the quality gap between answers; weakly related to prompt length.
limits: Exploratory; bias patterns judge-specific so no single fix.
agent_relevance: Position effects matter most when answers are close in quality, which is when the judgment matters most. Use order-swapped repeats on close calls.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Accuracy is highest when the answer passage is first or last in the context and drops in the middle (U-shape).
numbers: Multi-document QA: GPT-3.5-Turbo accuracy falls by more than 20 points in the worst position; with 20 and 30 documents it falls below the closed-book 56.1%. 30 docs: GPT-3.5-Turbo (16K) 73.4% at index 0, 50.5% at index 9, 63.7% at index 29. Claude-1.3 59.1% first, 54.8% mid, 59.9% last.
limits: 2023 models; newer long-context models may differ. Synthetic distractor setup.
agent_relevance: Put the key evidence at the start or end of the prompt. Do not bury it in a long context.

source: Jones & Steinhardt (2022) Capturing Failures of Large Language Models via Human Cognitive Biases
finding: Codex and GPT-3 show framing, anchoring and frequency effects, found by borrowing human-bias experiments.
numbers: Codex accuracy drops from 50% to 17% when the same task is described binary-first instead of unary-first; 75% of the wrong binary-first outputs equal the unary-first answer. GPT-3 reproduces the Asian disease direction: chooses the risky option far more under the 'not save' frame.
limits: At higher probabilities GPT-3 chose the risky option under both frames. Old models.
agent_relevance: Order of operations in a task description is a layout effect; the model may output the more frequent related solution.

source: Echterhoff et al. (2024) Cognitive Bias in Decision-Making with LLMs (BiasBuster)
finding: Tests anchoring, status quo, framing, primacy and group attribution bias on LLMs in admissions-style decisions. Self-help debiasing works best.
numbers: 13,465 prompts. Mitigations: awareness, contrastive, counterfactual, few-shot, and self-help (model rewrites its own prompt to remove bias). In their table GPT-4 framing gap went from -0.405 baseline to -0.010 with self-help; awareness and contrastive prompts left it near baseline.
limits: My reading of the table columns may be off; effects differ by model and bias. Hypothetical admissions task.
agent_relevance: Telling the model to be unbiased is weak. Having the program strip the biasing frame from the prompt is stronger.

source: Cherep, Maes, Singh (2025) LLM Agents Are Hypersensitive to Nudges (arXiv 2505.11584)
finding: On a multi-attribute choice task from Callaway et al., LLMs accept default, suggestion and highlighting nudges far more than humans.
numbers: Without nudge, accept rate: humans 0.51; gpt-3.5 0.33; gpt-4o-mini 0.58. With default nudge: humans 0.88, gpt-3.5 0.99, Gemini 1.5 Flash 0.94. Human score about 172 points; most models 134 to 159, only Gemini 1.5 Pro (166) and Claude 3.5 Sonnet (170) matched humans in late-suggestion trials. 340 trials per condition and model; about 1 billion tokens.
limits: Single task family; 2024 models. A search summary says a PNAS 2026 version finds reasoning models restore human-like sensitivity only inconsistently (not opened).
agent_relevance: A default or suggestion in the prompt is accepted almost always. Keep defaults out of the model-facing prompt unless they are the right answer.

source: Cherep et al. (2025) prompting remedies
finding: Zero-shot chain of thought shifts choices but does not remove nudge sensitivity. Few-shot human examples align behaviour but still leave hypersensitivity.
numbers: Conditions BASE, COT, FEW-SHOT (12 example games: 6 control, 3 accepted, 3 declined). Optimal nudges fitted to a human resource-rational model also raised LLM performance for some models.
limits: Authors call the gap hypersensitivity because humans are already sensitive.
agent_relevance: Reasoning text is not a debiasing guard. The check must be outside the model.

source: Samuelson & Zeckhauser (1988) status quo bias, as used by Echterhoff et al.
finding: Original status quo studies gave people a current option (car brand, investment) and measured switching. Used as the template for LLM tests.
numbers: No numbers read from the original this session.
limits: Secondary description only.
agent_relevance: Status quo prompts (current plan is X) are testable on our agent.

source: Johnson & Goldstein (2003) organ donation defaults, as summarised in Mertens et al.
finding: Opt-out countries had much higher donor registration than opt-in countries.
numbers: About 60 percentage points higher registration in opt-out countries (stated in the Mertens intro).
limits: Cross-country data, not a randomised trial; registration is not donation. Original not read.
agent_relevance: Defaults are the textbook case but the mechanism in real policy is contested.

source: Tversky & Kahneman (1981) Asian disease framing, as described by Jones & Steinhardt
finding: Same outcomes framed as lives saved or lives lost flip preference between a sure and a risky option.
numbers: Scenario: save 200 of 600 for sure vs 1/3 chance to save all; or 400 die for sure vs 2/3 chance all die. Original percentages not read this session.
limits: Large-replication results (e.g. Many Labs) not checked: search budget ran out.
agent_relevance: Gain versus loss wording of the same task is a ready test for our agent.

source: Limits of Defaults: influence of decision time on default effects (PMC12478545)
finding: A paper on decision time and default effects exists, but the full-text download failed (153 bytes).
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Candidate for a later pass: does time pressure raise default use?

source: Cross-source synthesis: where nudge sizes sit
finding: Estimates of the average nudge effect span a wide range depending on bias correction and scale.
numbers: Raw d=0.43 to 0.45; Mertens moderate-bias d=0.31; severe-bias 0.08; RoBMA 0.04 to 0.11; at-scale field 1.4 pp (8.1% relative); bias-corrected academic 3.2 pp.
limits: Different units (d vs pp) and sources; not directly comparable.
agent_relevance: Prior for our agent: the average layout nudge is small. The risk is large effects in particular slots: first position, default, and middle burial.

source: Cross-source synthesis: LLM layout effects vs human nudge literature
finding: Human nudge effects shrink after correction, but LLM order and default effects are measured directly and are large.
numbers: LLM: 6 to 15 point accuracy swings (Zheng); 82.5% judge conflict (Wang); 20+ point middle-position drop (Liu); 0.88 vs 0.99 default acceptance (Cherep).
limits: Many LLM studies use 2023 models and may be partly fixed in newer ones; each is a single benchmark.
agent_relevance: Treat layout as a risk to control, not a lever to exploit. Counterbalance order, keep defaults neutral, aggregate over permutations.

source: Szaszi et al. as discussed in the Mertens reply
finding: Szaszi et al. reanalysis (Andrews-Kasy, WAAP, trim-and-fill) also gives smaller or null effects, and urges explaining when nudges work.
numbers: No numbers from the Szaszi letter itself; the letter was not opened.
quote: we need to understand when and where some nudges have huge positive effects and why others are not able to repeat those successes
limits: Second-hand through the reply.
agent_relevance: Moderators matter more than the mean: record task type, model and option count with every layout test.
